item.title: Installing authn-bridge
item.description:
The repository ships the unit and the user it runs as: packaging/systemd/authn-bridge.service and packaging/sysusers.d/authn-bridge.conf. Everything below runs as root unless it says otherwise.
/usr/local/bin/authn-bridge the binary
/etc/authn-bridge/*.hcl the configuration, read in name order; root:authn-bridge, 0750, files 0640
/var/lib/authn-bridge/ keys, the subject salt, the SQLite state, the certificates issued, the disabled list; authn-bridge, 0700
/run/authn-bridge/ the admin socket, when the configuration asks for one

The binary

A release carries authn-bridge-<os>-<arch> for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64, a SHA256SUMS manifest and a build provenance attestation per binary; verifying a download says how to check both. Or build it, which records the version in the binary:

$ go install github.com/go-authn/bridge/cmd/authn-bridge@v0.22.0
$ authn-bridge --version
authn-bridge version v0.22.0

The path matters: from v0.20.0 the program lives in internal/app and the command in cmd/authn-bridge, so go install github.com/go-authn/bridge@... builds nothing.

The user, and why it is not a dynamic one 

install -m 0755 authn-bridge-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge
install -D -m 0644 authn-bridge.conf /etc/sysusers.d/authn-bridge.conf
systemd-sysusers # creates the authn-bridge user and group
install -m 0644 authn-bridge.service /etc/systemd/system/authn-bridge.service
systemctl daemon-reload

install -d -m 0750 -o root -g authn-bridge /etc/authn-bridge
install -d -m 0700 -o authn-bridge -g authn-bridge /var/lib/authn-bridge

The unit names User=authn-bridge, not DynamicUser=. The signing key, the subject salt, the SAML key and the certificate authorities are made before the first start, live for years, and must keep one owner across reinstalls and restores from backup. A dynamic user gets its UID when the service starts.

The keys

Run keygen as the service’s user, so that it owns what it writes. It refuses to overwrite a file that is already there:

$ mkdir var/nfs-ca
$ authn-bridge keygen --key var/oidc.key --salt var/salt --ssh-ca var/ssh-ca --x509-ca var/nfs-ca
wrote var/ssh-ca; its public half, for go-fileshare's trusted_user_ca_file:
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIBNOYvUrAPdRTB+38aml+twPN+2k1shD3l62v8NxrIje go-authn-bridge-ca
wrote var/oidc.key
wrote var/nfs-ca/ca.crt and its key; the certificate is what go-fileshare trusts for NFS over TLS
wrote var/salt -- keep it: a new salt is a new subject for everybody
$ authn-bridge keygen --key var/oidc.key
authn-bridge: open var/oidc.key: file exists

On a server the paths are under /var/lib/authn-bridge, and the command is runuser -u authn-bridge -- authn-bridge keygen ....

flag writes for
--key an RSA 3072 key ID tokens (RS256), published at /jwks
--salt 32 random bytes every sub, which is an HMAC under it
--access-token-key a P-256 key access tokens signed ES256 instead, much shorter
--ssh-ca an Ed25519 key in OpenSSH format the SSH certificates and the KRL’s signature
--x509-ca DIR DIR/ca.key (P-256) and DIR/ca.crt, valid ten years, path length 0 NFS client certificates and the CRL

Back up the salt, and never change it

A new salt gives every person a new sub, and every relying party then sees a new person. The same goes for deleting it on uninstall.

The SAML key and certificate are made with openssl: they are what the federation registers and what every IdP encrypts to. The key must be RSA (IdPs encrypt to it with RSA-OAEP). It is not the TLS certificate, and does not change with it.

runuser -u authn-bridge -- sh -c 'umask 077; openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:3072 -nodes -days 3650 \
 -subj "/CN=login.example.org" \
 -keyout /var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.key -out /var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.crt'

The federation’s metadata signing certificate comes from the federation, and so does its SHA-256 fingerprint: take the fingerprint from the federation’s web page, never from the same download as the certificate. See the federation side.

The unit

What it grants, in short:

  • Type=exec, Restart=on-failure, RestartSec=5s, TimeoutStopSec=20s. The provider shuts its listener down within ten seconds of SIGTERM.
  • StateDirectory=, RuntimeDirectory= (both 0700) and ConfigurationDirectory= (0750), UMask=0077. With ProtectSystem=strict, everything else is read-only.
  • No capability (CapabilityBoundingSet= and AmbientCapabilities= empty), NoNewPrivileges=, PrivateUsers=, PrivateTmp=, PrivateDevices=, PrivateIPC=, ProtectHome=, the kernel, clock, hostname and control groups protected.
  • RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6: TCP for the listener, the metadata, an ACME CA and a database; a socket for the admin API.
  • SystemCallFilter=@system-service, minus @privileged @resources, refused with EPERM rather than a kill.

It waits for network-online.target, because the metadata is fetched before the provider listens.

systemctl enable --now authn-bridge
journalctl -u authn-bridge -n 20

The first line in the journal is the one shown on the overview.

Changes need a restart

The configuration is read once. The unit has no ExecReload=, so systemctl reload is refused rather than pretending. A SIGHUP (from logrotate, or habit) is caught, logged and ignored. Left to Go’s default it would kill the process, and systemd would count that as a clean exit that Restart=on-failure does not restart:

SIGHUP: ignored, nothing is reloaded; restart the service to apply a configuration change (TLS certificate files are re-read on their own)

TLS certificate files are the exception: they are re-read when they change.

Port 443

The default listener is 127.0.0.1:8080, behind a TLS reverse proxy, and needs no capability. To serve TLS itself on port 443 (cert_file or acme), the provider needs CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE and must leave the private user namespace, since a capability held inside it does not apply to the host’s network:

# /etc/systemd/system/authn-bridge.service.d/port-443.conf
[Service]
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
PrivateUsers=no

Upgrading, and going back

Back up /var/lib/authn-bridge first: it holds the keys and the salt, which cannot be made again. Keep the binary that works, install the new one, restart:

cp -p /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge.previous
install -m 0755 authn-bridge-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge
systemctl restart authn-bridge

Going back is the same with authn-bridge.previous. A newer release may ship a newer unit: compare it with yours, install it and systemctl daemon-reload before the restart.

Coming from bridge

The configuration is unchanged; only the command and the release assets were renamed. Change every unit, script, cron job and bearer_token_command that runs bridge. The log line and the error prefix now say authn-bridge, so an alert that matched bridge v0. must match authn-bridge v0.. Metric names (bridge_*), the bridge_state table and the user-side cache (go-authn-bridge in the user’s configuration directory, ~/.config on Linux) are unchanged, so authn-bridge token reuses the logins bridge cached.

item.title: authn-bridge
item.description:
People log in at their own university, through RENATER’s Fédération Éducation-Recherche or eduGAIN, and applications get an OpenID Connect token. The same login can also have an SSH key certified, an X.509 client certificate issued for NFS over TLS, an application password set for SMB and S3, or a WireGuard key registered. The provider can revoke what it issued, and it publishes signed lists of what it has revoked; an access token already handed out stays valid until it expires. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, one binary. These pages describe v0.22.0.

go install github.com/go-authn/bridge/cmd/authn-bridge@v0.22.0

authn-bridge keygen --key /var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc.key --salt /var/lib/authn-bridge/salt
authn-bridge metadata --config /etc/authn-bridge > sp.xml # register this with the federation
authn-bridge check --config /etc/authn-bridge
authn-bridge --config /etc/authn-bridge # serve

Before v0.20.0 the command was bridge. That is also iproute2’s /sbin/bridge, installed on practically every Linux system, and whichever came first on PATH won. The module path is still github.com/go-authn/bridge.

Why a bridge

A research federation speaks SAML. Its members are hundreds of identity providers, one per institution, listed in a signed metadata document the federation publishes. Applications written today want OpenID Connect, and trust one provider. authn-bridge is that one provider: a SAML service provider on one side, registered once with the federation, and an OpenID provider on the other.

A gateway decides who everybody is for every application behind it, so most of this program is refusals. It refuses metadata the federation did not sign, an assertion that names somebody from another institution’s domain, groups an IdP has no authority over, and a configuration that would let any of these through. A configuration that cannot be served safely does not start.

What it prints at startup 

$ authn-bridge --config etc/bridge-admin.hcl
authn-bridge v0.22.0: http://127.0.0.1:28473 on 127.0.0.1:28473
metrics on 127.0.0.1:28475
admin API on unix:///tmp/authn/run/admin.sock

This is a test provider on loopback (an http:// issuer is accepted only on a loopback host). It fetches the federation’s metadata before it listens. A provider that cannot name a single institution is one nobody can log in through, so without the metadata it exits rather than starts.

Where to go next

Installing it the user, the directories, the systemd unit, the keys
The configuration every block, check, and what is refused at startup
The federation side metadata, its signer’s fingerprint, scopes, and what an IdP may assert
Tokens ID tokens, access tokens, the device grant, application passwords, WireGuard keys
Certificates SSH certificates, the EuroHPC profile, X.509 client certificates for NFS
Revocation the signed KRL and CRL, and the Shared Signals transmitter
The admin API disabling a person or an institution, health and metrics

The lists it signs are read by authn-revokd for a plain sshd or a TLS server, and by go-fileshare, which checks them itself.

What it is not

  • One process. With a state block, refresh tokens and the access tokens honoured at /userinfo survive a restart. Logins in progress, codes and device grants do not. The state is written through and read at start, so two instances on one database would each miss what the other wrote.
  • No dynamic client registration, and no front- or back-channel logout.
  • No users or groups to add. People exist because their institution vouches for them, and their groups are what it asserts.

Licence

BSD-3-Clause.

item.title: The configuration
item.description:
One HCL file, or a directory of them: --config /etc/authn-bridge reads every *.hcl there in name order and merges them, and --config may be given more than once. The configuration is read at start and never again.

issuer = "https://login.example.org" # https; compared whole by every relying party
listen = "127.0.0.1:8080" # the default: plain HTTP behind a TLS proxy
signing_key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc.key" # authn-bridge keygen --key
subject_salt_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/salt" # authn-bridge keygen --salt; never change it
disabled_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/disabled.json"
certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json"

saml {
 key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.key"
 cert_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.crt"
 metadata_url = "https://pub.federation.renater.fr/metadata/fer/idps.xml"
 metadata_cert_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/metadata-signature-2026.pem"
 metadata_fingerprint = "68:2F:20:58:41:9E:D0:79:EB:FE:3C:27:D6:A4:A4:09:39:6F:AE:3F:10:5F:22:EA:04:0F:04:F3:78:2D:5C:C0"
}

state {
 driver = "sqlite" # or postgres, mysql
 dsn_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/state.dsn"
}

client "my-app" {
 secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/my-app.secret" # absent: a public client
 redirect_uris = ["https://app.example.org/callback"]
}

What is required is issuer, signing_key_file, subject_salt_file, a saml block with the five keys above, and at least one client. Everything else has a default or is off.

check, before a restart

check reads the configuration the way the server does, loads every key it names, fetches the federation’s metadata, and says what would be served:

$ authn-bridge check --config etc/bridge.hcl
issuer http://127.0.0.1:28473
SAML entity http://127.0.0.1:28473/saml
tls none (a reverse proxy in front)
federation 1 IdPs, 1 usable here, valid until 2026-10-18T09:46:24Z
client sftp (public, public subject, audience [sftp])
client efp (public, public subject, audience [efp])
client nfs (public, public subject, audience [nfs])

Usable here leaves out an IdP that saml { idps } does not list, and one the admin API has disabled: with the institution above disabled, the same command prints federation 1 IdPs, 0 usable here. An idps entry the federation does not list is refused here, though the server would start with it:

federation 1 IdPs, 0 usable here, valid until 2026-10-18T09:46:24Z
authn-bridge: idps names "https://idp.nowhere.example/idp", which the federation does not list

authn-bridge metadata prints the SAML metadata to register with the federation. See the federation side.

The top level

key default
issuer the provider’s name and the base of every URL. https, or http on a loopback host for testing; no query, no fragment; a trailing / is dropped
listen 127.0.0.1:8080 the public listener
cert_file, key_file serve TLS from these files, re-read when they change; together or not at all
acme serve TLS with a certificate from an ACME CA instead (below); not with cert_file
signing_key_file RSA, signs ID tokens (RS256); a P-256 key here is refused
access_token_key_file the signing key a P-256 key that signs access tokens ES256; refused if it is the signing key
retired_signing_key_files keys that signed before: still published at /jwks, never used to sign
subject_salt_file at least 32 bytes
code_lifetime 1m at most ten minutes (RFC 6749 4.1.2)
token_lifetime 1h access tokens
id_token_lifetime 5m ID tokens
trusted_proxies addresses or prefixes whose X-Forwarded-For is believed
requests_per_minute 120 logins, device grants and ACS posts an address may start a minute; 0 turns the limit off
disabled_file where disabled people and institutions are kept; without it, disabling is refused
certificates_file every certificate and WireGuard key issued; required with ssh_ca, x509_ca or wireguard

The blocks:

block page
saml, claims the federation side
client below, and tokens
state below
ssh_ca, x509_ca certificates
app_passwords, wireguard tokens
ssf revocation
admin, metrics the admin API
acme below

A client

key default
secret_file the client secret, at least 16 characters; absent, a public client
redirect_uris compared exactly, except that a loopback URI may change port (RFC 8252); http only on loopback
audience the client ID what its access tokens are addressed to
subject public or pairwise: a different sub for this client (OIDC Core 8.1)
name the client ID shown on the device confirmation page
device false the device grant (RFC 8628); such a client needs no redirect URI
refresh_lifetime off refresh tokens, and how long after the login they end
pkce required or or_nonce, for a confidential client only: a nonce instead of PKCE
id_token_claims false copy the released claims into the ID token as well (opkssh needs it)
ssh_certificates, ssh_* SSH certificates
x509_certificates NFS client certificates
app_passwords may set the person’s application password
wireguard_keys, wireguard_peers WireGuard
ssf_receiver, ssf_subject_format a Shared Signals receiver

A client with no redirect URI must be a device client, an SSF receiver or a WireGuard gateway, or there is nothing it could do.

state: what a restart must not forget 

state {
 driver = "postgres" # sqlite, postgres or mysql
 dsn_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/state.dsn"
}

Refresh token families, the refresh tokens and the retired ones, the access tokens honoured at /userinfo and for certificates, the SAML assertions already accepted and the logins already answered, the SSF streams and their undelivered events: written through to one table, bridge_state (created if missing), and read at start. A refresh token is kept as its SHA-256, never as itself. Without the block they live in memory, and a restart logs everybody out.

A login in progress is not in it. It travels in its own cookie, sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key derived from the subject salt, so the browser can neither read nor change it.

acme 

acme {
 accept_terms_of_service = true # the operator's agreement; no default
 cache_dir = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/acme"
 email = "noc@example.org"
 # directory_url = "..." # Let's Encrypt by default
 # eab_key_id = "..." # External Account Binding (GÉANT TCS / HARICA)
 # eab_hmac_key_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/harica-eab.key"
 # http_listen = ":80" # http-01, and a redirect to https
 # directory_ca_file = "..." # a private ACME CA's own TLS
}

The certificate is for the issuer’s host. cache_dir holds private keys, and the provider refuses to start on one another user could reach or re-point.

What is refused at startup

Each of these is the output of authn-bridge check on a configuration that asked for it. The server refuses the same configurations: each is read from the configuration and the files it names. The one refusal check adds is the idps entry the federation does not list, above: the server fetches the same metadata before it listens, but does not hold idps to it.

An issuer, a redirect, a secret that leak:

authn-bridge: issuer "http://login.example.org": an issuer is https (http only on loopback, for testing)
authn-bridge: client "web": redirect URI "http://app.example.org/callback": a code sent over cleartext http is a code anybody on the path has
authn-bridge: client "web": a secret of 5 characters is a password somebody can guess
authn-bridge: code_lifetime = 15m0s: an authorization code lives ten minutes at most

A name any institution could claim:

authn-bridge: claims: username = "uid" is not held to an IdP's scopes, so any IdP of the federation could name anybody: it needs saml { idps } to list exactly one IdP; with more, use eppn or subject_id
authn-bridge: claims: groups = "affiliation" carries no institution, so any IdP of the federation could grant any of its values: it needs saml { idps } to list exactly one IdP; with more, use scoped_affiliation

Something issued that could never be taken back:

authn-bridge: ssh_ca: certificates_file is required with ssh_ca or x509_ca: a certificate that is not recorded can never be revoked
authn-bridge: ssh_ca: validity = 200h0m0s: more than a week, and a certificate lives that long on every server its revocation has not reached
authn-bridge: ssf: needs a state block: a queue a restart empties loses revocations

A listener that should not be reachable:

authn-bridge: admin: control: listen address "127.0.0.1:9443" is TCP, which requires mutual TLS (loopback included: any local user can reach it); missing TLSCertFile, TLSKeyFile, ClientCAFile
authn-bridge: metrics: listen is the public listener; metrics have one of their own

A configuration that says one thing twice:

authn-bridge: saml: an external discovery service lists every IdP; with `idps` restricted, leave `discovery` out and this provider lists them itself
authn-bridge: client "sftp" is declared twice

The SSH profile’s own refusals are on certificates, and the federation’s on the federation side.

item.title: The federation side
item.description:
On this side authn-bridge is a SAML service provider. It is registered once with the federation (RENATER’s Fédération Éducation-Recherche, or eduGAIN), and it trusts the federation’s metadata: one signed document that lists every member IdP, their signing keys, and the domains each may vouch for. The SAML code is go-authn/saml.

saml {
 key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.key" # RSA: IdPs encrypt assertions to it
 cert_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.crt"

 metadata_url = "https://pub.federation.renater.fr/metadata/fer/idps.xml"
 metadata_cert_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/metadata-signature-2026.pem"
 metadata_fingerprint = "68:2F:20:58:41:9E:D0:79:EB:FE:3C:27:D6:A4:A4:09:39:6F:AE:3F:10:5F:22:EA:04:0F:04:F3:78:2D:5C:C0"

 discovery = "https://discovery.renater.fr/renater" # or leave it out for this provider's own list
 # idps = ["https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth"] # restrict; one entry skips the choice

 names = { fr = "Passerelle OIDC", en = "OIDC gateway" }
 technical_contact = "admin@example.org"
}
key default
entity_id the issuer + /saml this service provider’s name in the federation
key_file, cert_file the SP’s RSA key and certificate
metadata_url https://, file:// for a copy something else keeps, or http:// on loopback only
metadata_cert_file, metadata_fingerprint the federation’s signing certificate and its SHA-256 fingerprint, both required
discovery this provider’s own list an external discovery service to send people to
idps every IdP of the federation restrict login to these entity IDs
names, descriptions, information_url, privacy_statement_url, technical_contact the issuer’s host as the name what goes in the SP metadata

The metadata’s signer is pinned

The certificate that signs the metadata is a file on this host, and its SHA-256 fingerprint is written in the configuration. The certificate is checked against the fingerprint at every start, so a file replaced on disk is noticed rather than trusted:

authn-bridge: saml: fed/fed.crt is not the certificate with fingerprint 68:2F:20:58:41:9E:D0:79:EB:FE:3C:27:D6:A4:A4:09:39:6F:AE:3F:10:5F:22:EA:04:0F:04:F3:78:2D:5C:C0

A key that arrives over the same channel as the document it vouches for vouches for nothing. So the fingerprint comes from the federation’s web page, never from the download that brought the certificate:

openssl x509 -in /etc/authn-bridge/metadata-signature-2026.pem -noout -fingerprint -sha256

A document is refused

  • when it is not signed by that certificate, or is signed with SHA-1, or its signature covers another element than the root;

  • when it has no validUntil, or is past it. This is RENATER’s own metadata as it was published on 29 September 2026, read on 10 October:

    $ authn-bridge check --config v/renater-expired.hcl
authn-bridge: the federation's metadata: metadata expired at 2026-10-08T07:30:02Z

  • when its validUntil is more than 28 days away: a document valid for years is one a replay keeps alive for years;

  • when it is older than the one in use (an earlier validUntil). It is validly signed and not yet expired, so nothing else would refuse it, and it may be the one with a key since revoked, served by whoever stands on the path;

  • over plain http to anything but loopback. The signature would catch a change, but not a proxy that holds back the new document and keeps serving the old one.

Refreshing it

The metadata is fetched before the provider listens, then again at three quarters of the document’s cacheDuration, never sooner than five minutes nor later than twelve hours, and whenever the admin API’s RefreshMetadata asks. A refresh that fails keeps the last good copy, but only until its own validUntil. After that nothing is vouched for, every IdP disappears, and /readyz says the provider is not ready. A federation server briefly unreachable logs nobody out; one unreachable for days does not leave the provider trusting stale keys.

Within the document, an IdP is kept only if it speaks SAML 2.0 and publishes an HTTP-Redirect SingleSignOnService. An entity described twice is dropped altogether, since nothing says which description is right, and one member’s unreadable certificate leaves out that member, not the federation.

What each IdP may say

A federation has hundreds of members, and any of them could otherwise say it is alice@another-university.example. Every member’s metadata lists its shibmd:Scopes, the domains it may vouch for; a regular-expression scope is ignored, not honoured.

Identifiers. A scoped value (subject-id, pairwise-id, eduPersonPrincipalName, eduPersonScopedAffiliation) outside the asserting IdP’s scopes is dropped, and a value with more than one @ is not in any scope.

Groups. With more than one IdP allowed to log in, an eduPersonEntitlement or isMemberOf value is kept only if its namespace is one of that IdP’s scopes or under one:

value its namespace
urn:mace:<domain>:... <domain>
urn:geant:<domain>:... (AARC-G002) <domain>
https://<host>/... <host>
anything else none: dropped

Groups decide what a person may do, at every resource server and in every certificate, so a value nobody can place is not passed on. A community proxy that asserts groups for people of many institutions is named explicitly, by entity ID, with the prefixes it may assert:

claims {
 trusted_groups = {
 "https://proxy.eduteams.org/saml2/idp/metadata.php" = ["urn:geant:eduteams.org:"]
 }
}

With exactly one IdP in saml { idps }, that IdP is trusted for every value.

From an assertion to claims 

claims {
 username = "eppn" # preferred_username: eppn, subject_id, uid or mail
 groups = ["entitlement"] # groups: entitlement, scoped_affiliation, affiliation, is_member_of
}

uid and mail are not held to any scope, and affiliation (staff, student) names no institution. So each needs saml { idps } to list exactly one IdP; with more, they are refused at startup.

sub. The identifier behind it is taken in this order: subject-id, then pairwise-id, then eduPersonPrincipalName, then eduPersonTargetedID, then a persistent NameID whose qualifier is the IdP itself. It is qualified by the IdP’s entity ID, and sub is an HMAC-SHA256 of it under the subject salt: stable, not reversible, not an address. public is the same for every client, pairwise differs per client. An IdP that releases none of these is refused, since nobody could be recognised twice. Mail is never an identifier, and there is no email_verified: an IdP asserting an address is not anybody having verified that the person reads it.

What the request asks of the IdP. prompt=none becomes IsPassive, and an IdP with no session answers login_required. prompt=login and max_age=0 become ForceAuthn; for any other max_age, a person whose IdP authenticated them longer ago than that is sent back with ForceAuthn. acr_values becomes RequestedAuthnContext, and an IdP that answers with another context is refused: a client that asked for a second factor is never told it got one when it did not.

The SP metadata

authn-bridge metadata prints what to register with the federation, without fetching anything (the certificate is shortened here):

$ authn-bridge metadata --config etc/bridge.hcl
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<md:EntityDescriptor xmlns:md="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:metadata" xmlns:ds="http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#" xmlns:mdui="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:metadata:ui" xmlns:idpdisc="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:profiles:SSO:idp-discovery-protocol" xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion" entityID="http://127.0.0.1:28473/saml">
<md:SPSSODescriptor protocolSupportEnumeration="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol" AuthnRequestsSigned="false" WantAssertionsSigned="true">
<md:Extensions>
<mdui:UIInfo>
<mdui:DisplayName xml:lang="en">127.0.0.1:28473</mdui:DisplayName>
</mdui:UIInfo>
</md:Extensions>
<md:KeyDescriptor>

<ds:X509Data>
<ds:X509Certificate>MIIE…</ds:X509Certificate>
</ds:X509Data>
</ds:KeyInfo>

<md:EncryptionMethod Algorithm="http://www.w3.org/2009/xmlenc11#aes256-gcm"/>

<md:AttributeConsumingService index="0">

<md:RequestedAttribute Name="urn:oid:1.3.6.1.4.1.5923.1.1.1.6" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:uri"/>
<md:RequestedAttribute Name="urn:oid:0.9.2342.19200300.100.1.3" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:uri"/>

</md:SPSSODescriptor>
</md:EntityDescriptor>

Assertions must be signed (WantAssertionsSigned="true"), and are delivered to /saml/acs by HTTP-POST. The same document is served at /saml/metadata.

What is refused

At the ACS, everything go-authn/saml refuses: an unsigned or SHA-1 assertion, several assertions, a replayed one, an identifier in a foreign scope. Then this provider’s own refusals:

  • an IdP response delivered into another browser: the login is found through its own sealed cookie, never through the RelayState the response carries; otherwise anybody could send their own IdP response to somebody else’s browser and log that person in under the sender’s identity;
  • an IdP that the configuration no longer allows, or that the admin API has disabled;
  • a person or an institution disabled here, whatever the institution says.

At startup, a list of IdPs together with RENATER’s discovery service, which lists them all and cannot be restricted:

authn-bridge: saml: an external discovery service lists every IdP; with `idps` restricted, leave `discovery` out and this provider lists them itself

item.title: Tokens, passwords and keys
item.description:
Every credential here starts with the same login at the person’s institution. What differs is who the credential is for, and how it is taken back. The certificates are on their own page.

What the provider publishes 

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .
{
"authorization_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/authorize",
"authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported": true,
"claims_parameter_supported": false,
"claims_supported": [
"sub",
"iss",
"aud",
"exp",
"iat",
"auth_time",
"nonce",
"acr",
"name",
"given_name",
"family_name",
"preferred_username",
"email",
"groups",
"eduperson_principal_name",
"eduperson_scoped_affiliation",
"eduperson_entitlement",
"entitlements",
"eduperson_assurance",
"eduperson_orcid",
"schac_home_organization",
"voperson_id"
],
"code_challenge_methods_supported": [
"S256"
],
"device_authorization_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/device_authorization",
"grant_types_supported": [
"authorization_code",
"refresh_token",
"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"
],
"id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": [
"RS256"
],
"issuer": "http://127.0.0.1:28473",
"jwks_uri": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/jwks",
"request_parameter_supported": false,
"request_uri_parameter_supported": false,
"response_modes_supported": [
"query"
],
"response_types_supported": [
"code"
],
"scopes_supported": [
"openid",
"profile",
"email",
"eduperson",
"groups"
],
"subject_types_supported": [
"public",
"pairwise"
],
"token_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/token",
"token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": [
"client_secret_basic",
"client_secret_post",
"none"
],
"userinfo_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/userinfo"
}

The authorization code flow, with PKCE S256 required for every client. A request with no code_challenge_method is refused rather than read as S256, since RFC 7636 makes plain the default. A confidential client configured pkce = "or_nonce" may send an OpenID nonce instead.

The ID token

For the client, and about the login, not the person: RS256, aud the client ID, sub, auth_time, at_hash, the nonce when the request had one, and acr when the IdP said which authentication context it used. Lifetime id_token_lifetime, five minutes by default.

Nothing about the person is in it. The claims the scopes release are at /userinfo, as OIDC Core 5.4 says when an access token is issued, and one always is. A client whose ID token is itself the credential, such as opkssh, sets id_token_claims = true to have them copied in. An ID token is only issued for a request with the openid scope.

scope releases
profile name, given_name, family_name, preferred_username
email email (never email_verified)
eduperson eduperson_principal_name, eduperson_scoped_affiliation, eduperson_entitlement and entitlements, eduperson_assurance, eduperson_orcid, schac_home_organization, voperson_id (the SAML subject-id, lower-cased)
groups groups

The access token

For the resource servers in the client’s audience, as RFC 9068 describes: signed with signing_key_file (RS256) or access_token_key_file (ES256), typ: at+jwt, valid token_lifetime (an hour by default). It carries what a resource server needs to decide without asking anybody: preferred_username, groups, idp (the entity ID of the IdP that vouched), scope, client_id, and session_end when the IdP said when its session ends.

What it leaves out, and why

No auth_time and no acr, although RFC 9068 allows both. They stay in the ID token, where OIDC Core puts them. Nothing reads them from an access token: not this provider, which looks a token up by its jti, and not go-fileshare. An access token, however, is also pasted as an SSH keyboard-interactive answer (ssh-oidc’s mccli, checked by motley-cue at /userinfo), and OpenSSH reads 1023 characters of one; an IdP’s acr alone, urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PasswordProtectedTransport, is about 90 of them. Before v0.22.0 the access token carried both.

The length of an ES256 access token (access_token_key_file) for a long eppn and three AARC entitlements, measured by authn-bridge’s TestES256AccessTokens with an issuer of a real length, against the shibmd:Scope lengths of RENATER’s metadata (743 scopes):

scope length characters
13 median 885
22 95th percentile 945
29 99th percentile 992
44 the longest 1092: over

Before v0.22.0 the same token was 1014 / 1074 / 1121 / 1221 characters: over from the 95th percentile on. What still does not fit is the longest scopes and, above all, many groups: every entitlement adds its whole URN, and nothing bounds how many an IdP sends. An RS256 access token, signed with a 3072-bit key, is about 1150 characters before any group, so a token meant for SSH is signed ES256. Past 1023 characters, mccli asks motley-cue for a one-time password instead, which motley-cue allows by default; a token pasted into plain ssh has to fit.

A token holding one of the provider’s own scopes (ssh, nfs, app_password, wireguard, wireguard_peers) is addressed to the provider alone: its aud is the issuer, and those endpoints refuse any other. A token a resource server received cannot be replayed here:

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/certificate -d x -D - -o -
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Www-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Date: Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:48:07 GMT
Content-Length: 23
the token is not valid

An access token already handed out is a signed statement a resource server checks on its own. What RevokePerson ends is everything that comes back here with it; the resource server learns from Shared Signals.

Without a browser: the device grant

A WebDAV client, a script, a terminal has no browser to send to a university. A client with device = true asks for a code (RFC 8628), and the person logs in on any other device:

client "rclone" {
 device = true
 audience = ["fileshare"]
 refresh_lifetime = "720h" # refresh tokens, off unless set
 name = "rclone (WebDAV)"
}

authn-bridge token --issuer https://login.example.org --client rclone prints an access token, logging in the first time and refreshing after that; it is golang.org/x/oauth2’s device client, not one written here.
user codes eight letters from BCDFGHJKLMNPQRSTVWXZ (no vowels, no digits), valid ten minutes; ten wrong codes per host in that time (an IPv4 address, an IPv6 /64), and ten times as many for the /24 or /48 around it
polling every five seconds; polling faster earns slow_down
waiting devices at most 20,000; past that the oldest is pushed out rather than everybody refused
refresh tokens rotated at every use, inside a family whose end is fixed at the login by refresh_lifetime; a retired one used again revokes the family and the access tokens it bought

Application passwords

NTLMv2 and SigV4 prove a secret the server must already hold, so no token will do for SMB or S3. A client with app_passwords = true lets a token with the app_password scope set one, generated and shown once: authn-bridge app-password --issuer ... --client files (--remove deletes it).

app_passwords {
 driver = "sqlite" # sqlite, postgres or mysql
 dsn_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/apppw.dsn"
 store = ["nt_hash"] # the default, SMB only; add "password" for S3
 lifetime = "2160h" # the default, 90 days
 # table = "app_passwords" # the default
}

The table is created if missing: login, password, nt_hash, expires, idp. Only what the protocols need is stored: the NT hash for SMB, the password itself only when store asks for it. go-fileshare reads it with a users "sql" block; name the columns in its query, never *.

Disabling a person removes their password; disabling an institution removes its people’s. A removed password stops working in go-fileshare when it next reads its directory.

WireGuard keys

WireGuard authenticates a peer by its public key and nothing else: no certificate, no expiry, no revocation. So the provider keeps the answer to whose is this key, and may it still connect? The device’s VPN client registers the public key, for a lease; the private key never leaves the device; a gateway reads the live keys as a list signed for it alone.

certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json" # keys are recorded beside the certificates

wireguard {
 lifetime = "24h" # the default: how long a key is listed; registering again renews it
 max_keys = 10 # the default: devices per person
}

client "vpn" { # what people log in with
 device = true
 wireguard_keys = true
}

client "vpn-gw" { # the gateway's own client
 secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/vpn-gw.secret"
 wireguard_peers = ["vpn"] # the clients whose keys it reads
 ssf_receiver = true # optional: told at once when somebody is disabled
}
POST /wireguard/key {"public_key": "...", "device": "laptop"}, with a token of the wireguard scope; answers the lease’s end
DELETE /wireguard/key {"public_key": "..."}: the owner takes a key back
GET /wireguard/peers for the gateway’s own client_credentials token, scope wireguard_peers: a signed JWT of type wireguard-peers+jwt, addressed to that gateway, valid five minutes

A key somebody else holds, a key that was taken back, and one key too many are refused with 409. A gateway client must be confidential, and must name clients that have wireguard_keys. The format of the list, and the gateway’s side, are go-authn/wireguard’s.

OpenPubkey and opkssh

opkssh turns an ID token into SSH logins with no CA at all, and the token it makes (a PK Token) outlives the ID token inside it. The provider returns the nonce verbatim in the code flow and in the device flow, signs RS256, and keeps a retired key published for as long as retired_signing_key_files names it, so that a PK Token signed before a rotation still verifies:

retired_signing_key_files = ["/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc-2026-03.key"]

Give opkssh a client of its own with id_token_claims = true: it matches people on the PK Token’s claims, and its ID token travels to every server it logs into.

item.title: Certificates
item.description:
A person who logged in can have an SSH public key certified, or an X.509 client certificate issued, for a few hours. A server that trusts the provider’s CA lets them in with no account file to edit there. Every certificate is recorded in certificates_file before it is handed out: one that cannot be recorded is not issued, since it could never be revoked, and revoked ones are published in the KRL and the CRL.

SSH certificates 

certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json"

ssh_ca {
 key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/ssh-ca" # authn-bridge keygen --ssh-ca; Ed25519
 validity = "12h" # the default; a week at most
}

client "sftp" {
 device = true
 ssh_certificates = true
}

authn-bridge ssh-cert --issuer https://login.example.org --client sftp logs in with a code, posts ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (or --key) to /ssh/certificate with a token of the ssh scope, and writes <key>-cert.pub beside it, where ssh and sftp find it.

The CA key must be Ed25519: an RSA CA key signs with SHA-1 unless told otherwise, which OpenSSH has refused by default since 8.8.

What the certificate says.

  • Exactly one principal, the person’s preferred_username unless the client’s profile says another claim. A certificate with no principal is valid for any user (PROTOCOL.certkeys), so a person with no username gets none. A name holding a comma, a space, a quote, a backslash or a control character is refused (403): sshd reads principals="a,b" and AuthorizedPrincipalsFile entries as lists, so one such name is two.
  • Key ID <principal> sub=<sub> jti=<token id>: what sshd logs.
  • No permit-* extension by default. SFTP needs none, and a certificate that permits no pty, no forwarding and no rc file grants file access and nothing else.
  • The person’s groups in the groups@go-authn.org extension, one per line, when the token carries groups. OpenSSH ignores it; it is signed, so a server that authorizes by group can believe it.
  • Valid from five minutes ago (for clocks that disagree) until validity from now, or until the IdP’s session ends if that is sooner.
  • The key must be Ed25519, ECDSA P-256/384/521, a security key (sk-), or RSA of at least 2048 bits. A certificate is refused as a key.

The EuroHPC SSH CA profile

The EuroHPC Federation Platform’s SSH CA (GÉANT / MyAccessID) issues Ed25519 certificates valid one hour, with one principal that names the person across the federation, and the hosts they are meant for in GÉANT’s ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org extension. A client can have its certificates issued in that shape. Every key is per client and optional; a client that sets none gets the certificate above.

client "efp" {
 device = true
 ssh_certificates = true
 ssh_principal_claim = "voperson_id" # the default is preferred_username
 ssh_validity = "1h" # never longer than ssh_ca's, nor the IdP's session
 ssh_extensions = ["permit-pty"] # none by default
 ssh_domain_grants = ["login.hpc.example.org"] # the hosting entity's hosts
 # ssh_source_address = ["192.0.2.0/24"] # the source-address critical option
}
key
ssh_principal_claim preferred_username, sub, voperson_id or eduperson_principal_name. The last two are released by the eduperson scope, which the token must hold (authn-bridge ssh-cert --scope eduperson); otherwise, or when the IdP released no such attribute, the answer is 403 saying which
ssh_extensions among permit-pty, permit-user-rc, permit-port-forwarding, permit-agent-forwarding, permit-X11-forwarding
ssh_source_address addresses or CIDR prefixes, written canonically into source-address
ssh_validity never longer than ssh_ca’s validity (equal is accepted), for this client
ssh_domain_grants domain patterns, checked by go-authn/sshcert’s ValidatePattern and encoded by its EncodeDomainGrant

What the profile refuses

Each at startup, from authn-bridge check:

authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_validity = 24h0m0s: longer than the ssh_ca validity, 12h0m0s
authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_extensions: "no-touch-required" is not one of permit-X11-forwarding, permit-agent-forwarding, permit-port-forwarding, permit-pty, permit-user-rc
authn-bridge: client "src": ssh_source_address: "192.0.2.1/24" has bits set under its mask: 192.0.2.0/24?
authn-bridge: client "x": ssh_principal_claim, ssh_extensions, ssh_source_address, ssh_validity and ssh_domain_grants shape SSH certificates: they need ssh_certificates = true

no-touch-required is not offered: it waives the user-presence test of the person’s own security key, which is not the provider’s to give away for everybody of a client.

A domain grant is held to the specification’s syntax, then to this provider’s own policy: lower case, at least two labels, and a wildcard only under a registrable domain. What stays fixed to the right of the last wildcard must not be a public suffix (the Public Suffix List): *.ac.uk would grant every institution under it.

authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_domain_grants: "*.ac.uk": a wildcard over the public suffix "ac.uk" grants every domain under it
authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_domain_grants: "Login.hpc.example.org": written in lower case, as hosting entities' domains are compared
authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_domain_grants: "login.hpc.*": sshcert: invalid domain pattern: pattern "login.hpc.*" has a wildcard in its rightmost label

Trusting it from a site

GET /ssh/config publishes the CA key in the shape EFP publishes its own, so a site follows EFP’s trust instructions with this provider’s URL:

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/config
{"PublicKey":"ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIBNOYvUrAPdRTB+38aml+twPN+2k1shD3l62v8NxrIje"}
curl -s https://login.example.org/ssh/config | jq -r '.PublicKey' > /etc/ssh/bridge-ssh-ca.pub
echo "TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/bridge-ssh-ca.pub" >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config

sshd ignores the domain grant. The site filters by it with an AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand: sshcert-authorize, which refuses a certificate whose grant does not name the host, and one with no grant at all. The CA is not in the OpenID discovery document: no OpenID Connect metadata names an SSH CA.

What remains different from EFP’s own CA: with ssh_principal_claim = "voperson_id", as above, the principal is the subject-id the person’s institution released, in lower case, not a MyAccessID identifier; the groups extension is there when the token carries groups; and there is a KRL, GET /ssh/krl, listing the certificates of people disabled here.

X.509 client certificates, for NFS over TLS

NFS over TLS (RFC 9289) can name the client by its certificate.

certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json"

x509_ca {
 key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/nfs-ca/ca.key" # authn-bridge keygen --x509-ca /var/lib/authn-bridge/nfs-ca
 cert_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/nfs-ca/ca.crt" # what go-fileshare trusts
 validity = "12h" # the default; a week at most
}

client "nfs" {
 device = true
 x509_certificates = true
}

authn-bridge nfs-cert --issuer ... --client nfs makes a P-256 key on the person’s machine, posts a certificate request to /x509/cert with a token of the nfs scope, and writes the certificate and the key. The CA key must be P-256, and its certificate a CA that signs certificates and CRLs.

What the certificate says. The request’s subject and extensions are ignored: what is certified is the token’s person, not what they asked for.

  • The person, user@domain, as one subjectAltName otherName 1.3.6.1.4.1.2238.1.1.1 holding a UTF8String, where FreeBSD’s rpc.tlsservd -u reads it. A username without @, or under three bytes, is refused.
  • Each group as a URI name beside it: tag:go-authn.github.io,2026:group:<the group, percent-encoded>.
  • The CN is the username; past 64 characters the subject is empty and the subjectAltName critical (RFC 5280).
  • Client authentication only, and a CRL distribution point: <issuer>/x509/crl.
  • Valid from five minutes ago until validity, the IdP’s session or the CA’s own certificate, whichever ends first.
  • A P-256 or RSA (2048 bits and more) key, and a request signed by it.

A certificate names the machine, not the user of it

RFC 9289: the server “cannot utilize the remote TLS peer identity to authenticate RPC users”. Linux sets the client certificate per mount, so everybody using that mount is the person it names. This is for a machine one person uses, and authn-bridge nfs-cert says so.

A certificate request held open across a disabling

The token is checked when the request starts and the body read after, at whatever pace the client sends it. So a certificate is recorded first, and then the token and the person are checked again: if the person was disabled, or the token revoked, in between, the certificate just recorded is revoked and the answer is 401. Either the revocation saw the certificate, or the certificate sees the revocation.

item.title: What it revokes, and how servers hear of it
item.description:
Disabling a person or an institution (the admin API) ends everything that comes back to the provider: refresh tokens, /userinfo, new certificates, application passwords. What it has already handed out is checked elsewhere, against keys, and three mechanisms reach it:

credential taken back by
an SSH certificate this CA signed the KRL, GET /ssh/krl, with its signature at /ssh/krl.sig
an X.509 client certificate the CRL, GET /x509/crl
an access token, an opkssh certificate, anything a server verifies alone a Shared Signals session-revoked event

Revocation is permanent. Enabling a person again does not bring their certificates back; they get new ones. A list a revocation could be taken out of is a list somebody who reaches the admin API could edit.

The lists

Both are issued as go-authn/revocation’s protocol says, so that they can travel through anything (a mirror, plain HTTP, a file) and still be checked by whoever reads them:

KRL CRL
format OpenSSH PROTOCOL.krl, written by go-authn/krl: what sshd’s RevokedKeys and ssh-keygen -Q read DER, RFC 5280
signed a detached SSHSIG by the SSH CA key, namespace krl@go-authn.github.io by the CA that signs the certificates
current until its expires@go-authn.github.io extension (which sshd ignores) its nextUpdate
ordered by its krl_version, then its generation date its CRL Number, then thisUpdate

Each list says it stops being current an hour after it is issued. A list is kept and served unchanged until it is half way to that, or until something is revoked; the next request then gets a new issue. An issue is never dated before the one it replaces, even if the clock steps back, since a reader refuses an earlier issue of the same version as a rollback. The CRL Number rises at every issue.

The KRL from a test provider with nothing revoked:

$ curl -s -D - -o var/bridge.krl http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: max-age=60
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Etag: "db5b4e920d2da3911da51a8f70db8c4f"
Date: Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:48:14 GMT
Content-Length: 130
$ ssh-keygen -Q -l -f var/bridge.krl
# KRL version 0
# Generated at 20261011T114814
# Comment: go-authn/bridge http://127.0.0.1:28473

The ETag is the content’s. A reader polls with If-None-Match, and gets 304 while the issue it holds is still the one served; since the content changes at least every half hour, a polling reader never keeps a copy past its expiry:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -H 'If-None-Match: "db5b4e920d2da3911da51a8f70db8c4f"' -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl
304

The signature is fetched with If-Match on the list’s ETag. A list issued again in between answers 412, rather than a signature that does not match it:

$ curl -s -o var/bridge.krl.sig -H 'If-Match: "db5b4e920d2da3911da51a8f70db8c4f"' -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl.sig
200
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -H 'If-Match: "stale"' -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl.sig
412

ssh-keygen checks the signature, and refuses it in any other namespace:

$ ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed -I bridge -n krl@go-authn.github.io -s bridge.krl.sig < bridge.krl
Good "krl@go-authn.github.io" signature for bridge with ED25519 key SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q

where allowed is the line bridge namespaces="krl@go-authn.github.io" <the CA key from /ssh/config>.

The CRL, issued fifteen seconds later:

$ openssl crl -inform DER -in var/bridge.crl -noout -text
Certificate Revocation List (CRL):
Version 2 (0x1)
Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA256
Issuer: CN=go-authn bridge NFS client CA
Last Update: Oct 11 09:48:29 2026 GMT
Next Update: Oct 11 10:48:29 2026 GMT
CRL extensions:
X509v3 Authority Key Identifier:
2A:90:7A:50:FF:65:52:BA:70:4E:E1:F8:70:EE:7A:FC:B1:8B:FE:4E
X509v3 CRL Number:
1791712109993
No Revoked Certificates.
Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA256
Signature Value:
30:44:02:20:37:90:14:6f:c1:f2:ea:98:29:04:61:88:a8:17:
88:e3:f6:84:9d:46:a7:fc:2b:ac:81:26:47:9d:ac:84:23:38:
02:20:0a:a6:93:cb:7d:2d:81:e4:59:d4:0d:a0:fd:f4:6e:75:
c9:0d:53:e7:92:49:ac:a1:31:a8:90:09:91:d1:87:b6

A certificate stays in its list until it expires: an expired certificate is refused everywhere without being listed.

Who reads them

  • A plain sshd, or nginx and other TLS servers: authn-revokd fetches the lists, keeps only those that verify, writes them where the servers read them, and fails closed for sshd when a list lapses.
  • go-fileshare fetches and verifies them itself, and refuses the provider’s certificates while it holds no current list.

Shared Signals

An access token or an opkssh certificate is checked where it is used, and no list can name it. So the provider is an OpenID Shared Signals transmitter: on DisablePerson, RevokePerson and DisableIdP it queues a CAEP session-revoked event (everything issued to this subject before the event’s time is void) for every receiver that asked.

state { ... } # required: a queue a restart empties loses revocations
ssf {} # event_retention = "192h" by default

client "fileshare-ssf" { # a receiver: client credentials, scope ssf
 secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/fileshare-ssf.secret"
 ssf_receiver = true
 audience = ["fileshare"]
}
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/.well-known/ssf-configuration | jq .
{
"issuer": "http://127.0.0.1:28473",
"jwks_uri": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/jwks",
"delivery_methods_supported": [
"urn:ietf:rfc:8936"
],
"configuration_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams",
"status_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/status",
"add_subject_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/subjects:add",
"remove_subject_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/subjects:remove",
"verification_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/verify",
"spec_version": "1_0",
"authorization_schemes": [
{
"spec_urn": "urn:ietf:rfc:6749"
}
]
}
  • Poll delivery only (RFC 8936): the receiver asks; nothing here dials out.
  • A receiver authenticates with an access token from the client credentials grant, for an ssf_receiver client with a secret, scope ssf. It sees its own streams only, ten at most.
  • Events are SETs (RFC 8417) signed with the ID token key, with no exp and no sub. The subject is the account, acct:<username>, by default: a sub may be pairwise, one per client. A receiver configured ssf_subject_format = "iss_sub" gets instead the issuer and the public sub.
  • An institution disabled is one event per person the provider has a trace of there, and one whose subject is the tenant, the institution’s entity ID, with its scopes, which covers the people the provider has forgotten.
  • Streams and undelivered events are kept in the state database until acknowledged or event_retention passes. An event a receiver reports in error is handed out again, up to ten times.

The SSF block is refused without a state block:

authn-bridge: ssf: needs a state block: a queue a restart empties loses revocations

item.title: The admin API, health and metrics
item.description:
Both are off unless the configuration asks for them, and neither is ever on the public listener.

admin {
 listen = "unix:///run/authn-bridge/admin.sock" # mode 0600
 # or over the network, mutual TLS and nothing less (loopback included):
 # listen = "10.0.0.5:9443"
 # tls_cert_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/admin.crt"
 # tls_key_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/admin.key"
 # client_ca_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/operators-ca.crt"
 # reflection = true # for grpcurl; off by default
}

metrics { listen = "127.0.0.1:9101" } # /healthz /readyz /metrics

disabled_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/disabled.json"

The listener is grpc-transports/control’s, shared with go-fileshare. The socket is never reachable by another user, not even between bind and chmod, and is never taken from an instance still running. TCP without all three TLS files is refused, loopback included, since every local user can reach 127.0.0.1:

authn-bridge: admin: control: listen address "127.0.0.1:9443" is TCP, which requires mutual TLS (loopback included: any local user can reach it); missing TLSCertFile, TLSKeyFile, ClientCAFile

A binary built with -tags nogrpc has no admin API, and refuses a configuration with an admin block rather than start without it.

The service

bridge.admin.v1.AdminService (proto/bridge/admin/v1/admin.proto), with grpc.health.v1 beside it, which reports SERVING while the provider is ready.
Status version, issuer, start time; the federation’s metadata (IdPs, usable, valid until, last refresh, last error); what is held in memory
RefreshMetadata fetch the federation’s metadata now, and say how it went
ListIdPs the federation’s IdPs, as the institution list shows them (query, limit, 100 by default)
ListClients the configured relying parties
RevokePerson end their refresh token families, the access tokens those bought, their logins and device grants in progress and their application password, and revoke everything the certificate store holds for them: SSH and X.509 certificates (into the next KRL and CRL) and WireGuard keys
DisablePerson, EnablePerson refuse somebody here, at login and at every token, whatever their institution says, and revoke what they hold; optionally until a time
DisableIdP, EnableIdP the same for everybody one institution vouches for; a metadata refresh does not lift it
ListDisabled who is disabled, why, by whom, since and until when

With reflection = true, against a test provider:

$ grpcurl -plaintext -unix $PWD/run/admin.sock bridge.admin.v1.AdminService/Status
{
"version": "v0.22.0",
"issuer": "http://127.0.0.1:28473",
"started": "2026-10-11T09:48:00.318671Z",
"federation": {
"metadataUrl": "file:///tmp/authn/fed/metadata.xml",
"idps": 1,
"usable": 1,
"validUntil": "2026-10-18T09:46:24Z",
"lastRefresh": "2026-10-11T09:48:00.319741Z"
},
"counts": {}
}

Disabling 

$ grpcurl -plaintext -unix -d '{"username":"alice@univ-example.example","reason":"left the lab"}' $PWD/run/admin.sock bridge.admin.v1.AdminService/DisablePerson
{
"disabled": {
"username": "alice@univ-example.example",
"reason": "left the lab",
"by": "uid=501",
"since": "2026-10-11T09:48:39.136975Z"
},
"revoked": {}
}
$ grpcurl -plaintext -unix -d '{"entity_id":"https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth","reason":"compromised","until":"2026-10-12T08:00:00Z"}' $PWD/run/admin.sock bridge.admin.v1.AdminService/DisableIdP
{
"disabled": {
"entityId": "https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth",
"reason": "compromised",
"by": "uid=501",
"since": "2026-10-11T09:48:39.192047Z",
"until": "2026-10-12T08:00:00Z"
},
"revoked": {}
}

revoked counts what each call ended (refresh families, access tokens, logins, application passwords, certificates); nothing was live here. Every call that changes something is logged with who made it, the peer’s uid= on the socket or the client certificate’s cn= over TLS:

disabled alice@univ-example.example (0 known identities) by uid=501 until enabled again: left the lab
revoked alice@univ-example.example: 0 refresh families, 0 access tokens, 0 logins, 0 app passwords, 0 certificates
disabled IdP https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth by uid=501 until 2026-10-12T08:00:00Z: compromised
revoked IdP https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth: 0 refresh families, 0 access tokens, 0 logins, 0 app passwords, 0 certificates
enabled alice@univ-example.example by uid=501

A person is disabled as who they are. Usernames compare without case, as eppn, uid, mail and subject-id all do, so the same call with "Alice@Univ-Example.example" lifts what was set for alice@univ-example.example ({"wasDisabled": true}). The entry also records the stable identity of everybody known under that name, so another spelling from their IdP does not let them back in. A name with no @ is also matched as a sub, for a person whose IdP releases no username.

The entry is recorded before anything is revoked, so a grant racing the revocation meets the entry.

Disabling is kept in disabled_file, and refused without one. Somebody disabled until the next restart would be let back in by the next deployment:

$ grpcurl -plaintext -unix -d '{"username":"alice@univ-example.example"}' $PWD/run/admin.sock bridge.admin.v1.AdminService/DisablePerson
ERROR:
Code: FailedPrecondition
Message: disabling needs disabled_file in the configuration: without it, a restart would forget who is disabled

A file that cannot be read stops the provider from starting, for the same reason. A disabled institution counts as not usable in Status, ListIdPs and check.

What disabling reaches beyond the provider is on revocation: the KRL and the CRL for certificates, Shared Signals for tokens. An application password removed here stops working in go-fileshare when it next reads its directory; call its ReloadDirectory after DisablePerson for the effect to be immediate.

What RevokePerson cannot end

An access token already handed out is a signed statement a resource server checks on its own, valid there until it expires (an hour by default). An SSH certificate already issued lasts its validity unless the server reads the KRL, which is why both are short.

Health and metrics

go-net-health/endpoint’s, as in go-fileshare, on the metrics listener, which must not be the public one (a configuration that makes it so is refused):
/healthz up while the process answers
/readyz ready while the federation’s metadata is loaded and within its validUntil, and no revocation is waiting to reach the state database
/metrics Prometheus text, bridge_* families 
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28475/metrics | grep "^bridge_"
bridge_build_info{version="v0.22.0",goversion="go1.27.2",revision="e1c4fdc3ae1cdddf2ccb4e64bda4317b5bf4f3a8"} 1
bridge_start_time_seconds 1791712080
bridge_ready 1
bridge_metadata_valid_until_timestamp_seconds 1792316784
bridge_metadata_idps 1
bridge_metadata_last_refresh_timestamp_seconds 1791712080
bridge_metadata_refreshes_total{result="failed"} 0
bridge_metadata_refreshes_total{result="ok"} 1
bridge_logins_in_progress 0
bridge_devices_waiting 0
bridge_refresh_families 0
bridge_access_tokens 0
bridge_disabled{kind="idp"} 0
bridge_disabled{kind="person"} 0
bridge_ssh_certificates_total 0
bridge_x509_certificates_total 0

The counters of logins by outcome (bridge_logins_total), of tokens by grant (bridge_tokens_issued_total) and of application passwords (bridge_app_passwords_total) appear only once they have counted something. No label names a person or an institution: which universities’ people use the service, and when, is not the provider’s to publish. Alert on bridge_metadata_valid_until_timestamp_seconds before the time it gives is reached: past it, nobody can log in.
